title: A/B Testing With 500 Users: What You Can Actually Detect (and What to Decide on Judgment)
text: Medium AB Testing Sample Size: What 500 Users Can Detect | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The only number that matters: the lift 500 users can detect The A/B test sample size formula, in code Why a small sample win is usually 2 to 4 times too big Peeking: 5 percent becomes 19 percent in ten looks Bayesian and sequential methods: what they fix and what they do not Where this thesis breaks: the honest caveats A kill rule: when to stop testing and ship on judgment FAQ: AB testing sample size The takeaway Sources AI Startup Data Science Ab Testing Product Management A/B Testing With 500 Users: What You Can Actually Detect (and What to Decide on Judgment) Syed Ali 15 min read · Nov 1, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Every test has a floor: below it, small lifts fall straight through. Image created by the author with AI. AB testing sample size for startups with hundreds of users decides what a test can see before it runs. At 500 users per arm, modest lifts are invisible, and the wins that do clear the bar are usually inflated. With 500 users in each arm and a 10 percent baseline conversion rate, an A/B test can only reliably detect a lift of about 60 percent. That is not a typo, and it is the number most startup experiment advice leaves out. The guides were written for sites with a million visitors, and most AI products I see ship weekly to cohorts of a few hundred. Before you read a result from a test that small, it helps to know what it was ever able to see. That is the sample size problem. Every test has a floor, and below it the dashboard still prints a winner. Before Echonos I worked as a data science consultant at Deloitte, Booz Allen Hamilton and Accenture, and later ran operations as COO at Tabler. The habit those years left me with is unglamorous. Before I trust a result, I ask what the test could have detected if the idea had worked. When the honest answer is “only a miracle”, the result is a coin flip with a confidence interval drawn around it. This piece is for founders, product managers and data people who test on hundreds or low thousands of users. With a million weekly visitors and a platform team, you can skip to the caveats. With small cohorts, read on, because the arithmetic decides more of your roadmap than you think. It helps to separate three questions a test can answer, because small teams blur them. The first question is detection. Did the test have enough users to notice an effect of the size you care about? This is set before launch by the baseline, the sample and the lift. The second question is size. How big is the effect? A test can detect something and still report its size badly. The third question is sign. Is the effect even positive? At very low power a “significant” result can point the wrong way. The common confusion is between the first two. Teams treat “it was significant” as proof that the measured lift is the real lift. At small samples those are different claims. The only number that matters: the lift 500 users can detect The short answer: with a 10 percent baseline, 80 percent power and a 5 percent significance level, you need about 3,841 users in each arm to detect a 20 percent relative lift. With 500 per arm, the smallest lift you can reliably detect is about 60 percent. Smaller lifts are mostly invisible. That figure is the minimum detectable effect, and it is the one number worth computing before any test. I reran it for this piece with the standard two sided, two proportion z test. The formula, per arm: n = (z(1 − α/2) × √(2 × p̄ × (1 − p̄)) + z(power) × √(p1 × (1 − p1) + p2 × (1 − p2)))² ÷ (p2 − p1)² Here p1 is the baseline, p2 is the baseline times one plus the relative lift, and p̄ is their average. With α at 0.05 and power at 0.80, the two z values are 1.96 and 0.84. The figures below work as a calculator for most startup cases: users needed in each arm, by baseline, for each relative lift in brackets. 2% baseline: 315,206 (5%), 80,682 (10%), 21,109 (20%), 9,798 (30%), 3,826 (50%) 5% baseline: 122,124 (5%), 31,234 (10%), 8,158 (20%), 3,780 (30%), 1,471 (50%) 10% baseline: 57,763 (5%), 14,751 (10%), 3,841 (20%), 1,774 (30%), 686 (50%) 20% baseline: 25,583 (5%), 6,510 (10%), 1,683 (20%), 772 (30%), 294 (50%) 30% baseline: 14,856 (5%), 3,763 (10%), 963 (20%), 437 (30%), 163 (50%) Read it the other way and it gets uncomfortable. At 500 users per arm the detectable relative lift is about 92% on a 5 percent baseline, 60% on a 10 percent baseline and 38% on a 20 percent baseline. At 200 per arm it is about 160%, 100% and 61%. Even at 1,000 per arm it is about 62%, 41% and 26%. Press enter or click to view image in full size At 500 users per arm, the smallest detectable lift is 92%, 60% and 38% at 5%, 10% and 20% baselines. Animation created by the author with AI. The mechanism is simple. Noise shrinks with the square root of the sample, so halving the lift you want to detect roughly quadruples the users you need. Lower baselines are worse, because the signal is a small difference between two small numbers. Published guidance agrees from bigger sites. Tomasz Tunguz wrote in 2016 that a 20 percent change on a 3 percent baseline at 90 percent confidence needs about 12,000 users per variation; my recompute gives about 11,000 to 15,000 depending on power. Georgi Georgiev at Analytics Toolkit wrote in 2019 that a standard setup “needs roughly 50,000 to 500,000 users.” The A/B test sample size formula, in code Short enough to paste into a notebook, and it uses only the Python standard library: from math import sqrt, ceil from statistics import NormalDist def users_per_arm(baseline, relative_lift, alpha=0.05, power=0.80): """Two sided, two proportion z test. Returns users needed in EACH arm.""" z_a = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2) z_b = NormalDist().inv_cdf(power) p1 = baseline p2 = baseline * (1 + relative_lift) pbar = (p1 + p2)
